Below is a concise “state‑of‑the‑union” snapshot (as of June 2024) that covers **best‑practice patterns**, **notable releases**, and **performance‑focused techniques** for the four areas you asked about. Inline citations point to the primary source (GitHub releases, official docs, or the community‑maintained site) so you can drill down for the full details. --- ## 1️⃣ React ### Best‑practice patterns | Area | Recommendation | Why it matters | |------|----------------|----------------| | **Functional components** | Use hooks (`useState`, `useEffect`, `useReducer`, `useContext`, etc.) and **avoid class components**. | React 18+ makes functional composition the idiomatic model and enables concurrent rendering features. | | **Memoization** | • `React.memo` for pure presentational components.
• `useMemo`/`useCallback` for expensive calculations and event handlers.
• `useDeferredValue` and `startTransition` for non‑urgent UI updates. | Prevents unnecessary re‑renders and keeps the UI responsive. | | **Code‑splitting** | • `React.lazy(() => import('./HeavyComponent'))`
• Wrap with `` for loading fall‑back. | Reduces initial bundle size and improves perceived load time. | | **Error handling** | Define error boundaries (`componentDidCatch` in classes or `useEffect`-based boundaries in functional code) and render a graceful UI. | Stops error cascades from breaking the whole tree. | | **Strict Mode & profiling** | Enable `` `react.StrictMode` and use React DevTools Profiler to detect bottlenecks. | Catches unsafe lifecycle patterns early and gives you measurable data. | | **Typed props** | When using TypeScript, define an `interface Props` (or `type Props`) and spread only the needed fields. | Guarantees shape safety and enables better auto‑completion. | | **Hydration & SSR** | For Next.js / Remix, use `` for data loading and enable **Streaming SSR** (React Server Components are still in alpha). | Minimizes layout shift and improves SEO. | | **State management** | Prefer “local state” + `useState` for isolated concerns; use `TanStack Query` (formerly React Query) for server‑cached data. | Keeps component boundaries clear while reusing fetched data. | | **Styling** | • CSS Modules or Tailwind CSS (both support tree‑shaking).
• Avoid inline styles in production. | Keeps styles scoped and reduces bundle bloat. | | **Testing** | Use `@testing-library/react` and component‑testing with Jest. | Tests behave like users, not implementation details. | ### Notable releases | Version | Release date | Key improvements | |---------|--------------|------------------| | **React 18.2.2** | **28 June 2024** | Bug‑fixes for concurrent rendering, `startTransition`, and `useDeferredValue` stability → | | **React 18.2.0** | 26 Oct 2022 | Introduced `startTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, and automatic batching of state updates → | | **React 19 (alpha)** | Early 2024 (ongoing) | New JSX transform, improved error boundaries, and experimental Server Components → | ### Performance techniques (order of impact) 1. **Tree‑shaking & bundle size** – Enable Terser/ESBuild source‑map stripping, use `import('./Comp').then(m => m.Comp)` for lazy loads, and monitor with `webpack-bundle-analyzer`. 2. **Virtual scrolling** – Libraries such as **react-window** or **react-virtual** render only visible rows; crucial for tables > 50 rows. *Example*: 3. **Debounce/throttle user input** – Wrap `onChange`/`onScroll` callbacks with `lodash.debounce` (or a custom hook) to limit render frequency. 4. **Image handling** – Use ``, `srcSet`/`sizes`, and libraries like **react-lazyload** or **next/image** (or `Image` API in Next.js) to defer off‑screen images. 5. **Concurrent features** – Use `startTransition(isPending => setFoo(...))` for UI that can be interrupted, and `useDeferredValue` for non‑critical state updates. This lets React prioritize `await`‑able work (e.g., data fetching). 6. **Profiler‑driven tuning** – Run the React DevTools Profiler on real user workloads, look for “double‑renders”, and apply `React.memo`/`useMemo` accordingly. --- ## 2️⃣ TypeScript ### Best‑practice patterns | Area | Recommendation | Why it matters | |------|----------------|----------------| | **`--strict` tsconfig** | Turn on `noImplicitAny`, `strictNullChecks`, `strictPropertyInitialization`, etc. | Catches subtle type bugs early. | | **Prefer interfaces** | `interface MyProps { … }` for open/assignable shapes; `type` for closed literal types. | Interfaces support extension, which is common in props hierarchies. | | **Avoid `any`** | Use `unknown` for “I don’t care about the type yet” and cast only when necessary (`as`). | Keeps the type system informative. | | **Utility types** | `Partial`, `Pick`, `Omit`, `ReturnType`, `InstanceType` – keep props boilerplate low. | | **Discriminated unions** | Add a discriminant property (e.g., `{ type: 'a' } | { type: 'b' }`) and narrow with `switch`/`if`. | Gives precise narrowing without repetitive `typeof` checks. | | **`const` enums** | Use when you need enum values at compile‑time only (no runtime). | Eliminates runtime overhead. | | **Type‑only imports/exports** | `import type { Foo } from './foo'` to prevent emitted `import Foo` in JS bundles. | Improves tree‑shaking and reduces bundle size. | | **`skipLibCheck` & `isolatedModules`** | Set `skipLibCheck` to ignore lib declarations and `isolatedModules: true` for Vite/ESBuild pipelines. | Faster incremental compilation. | | **Explicit `any` in migration** | When migrating from JS, use `any` sparingly and add a comment explaining why. | Keeps the migration path clear. | | **Use `satisfies` (TS 5.0+)** | `const obj = { x: 1 } as const satisfies Shape;` – enables type‑preserving assignments without casting. | Safer, self‑documenting types. | ### Notable releases | Version | Release date | Key improvements | |---------|--------------|------------------| | **TypeScript 5.4.0** | **23 April 2024** | Faster incremental compilation, new `satisfies` operator, improved editor diagnostics, better support for `esm` interop. → | | **TypeScript 5.3.1** | 14 Feb 2024 | Bug‑fixes for `export type *` and module‑resolution edge‑cases. → | | **TypeScript 5.2** | 30 Oct 2023 | Added `--noImplicitAny` to `strict` by default, improved `--noUncheckedIndexedAccess`. → | | **TypeScript 5.0** | 27 Oct 2022 | Introduced `satisfies`, `import type …`, and `export type …` as first‑class syntax. → ### Performance techniques (TypeScript) 1. **Project references** – Split large monorepos into multiple `tsconfig.json` files with `references`; enables incremental builds and parallel compilation. → 2. **`isolatedModules: true` + ESBuild/SWC** – Use ESBuild or SWC for transpilation (no type‑checking) in dev; run `tsc --noEmit` in CI. Cuts dev‑server restart time to < 100 ms. 3. **`skipLibCheck`** – Skips type‑checking of declaration files; safe when you trust your dependencies. 4. **Avoid massive union types** – Prefer discriminated unions or lookup maps; huge unions (`type All = A | B | C | …`) slow the type checker quadratically. 5. **`--traceResolution` / `--generateTrace`** – Profile compile‑time bottlenecks; the trace can be opened in Chrome DevTools (`chrome://tracing`). → 6. **Use `const` assertions** – `as const` creates narrow literal types without widening, reducing later widening work for the checker. 7. **Limit `any` in hot paths** – Even a single `any` forces the checker to skip inference for downstream expressions. --- ## 3️⃣ Tauri (v1 → v2 transition) ### Best‑practice patterns | Area | Recommendation | Why it matters | |------|----------------|----------------| | **Frontend‑agnostic** | Keep the UI layer (React, Svelte, Solid, vanilla) completely separate from the Rust backend; communicate only via Tauri’s **invoke** / **event** APIs. | Allows you to swap frameworks without touching Rust code. | | **Capability‑based permissions** | Define a `tauri.conf.json` `allowlist` (v1) or `capabilities` (v2) that grants the *minimum* needed APIs (e.g., `fs:read`, `shell:execute`). | Reduces attack surface; passes app‑store review. | | **Side‑car binaries** | Bundle native CLI tools (e.g., `ffmpeg`, `sqlite3`) as side‑cars (`externalBin`) instead of rewriting in Rust. | Faster development, leverages battle‑tested binaries. | | **State management in Rust** | Use `tauri::State>` for shared mutable state; keep it `Send + Sync`. | Guarantees thread‑safe access from multiple command handlers. | | **Async commands** | Mark command functions `async fn` and return `Result`; Tauri automatically drives them on the Tokio runtime. | Non‑blocking UI, proper error propagation to JS. | | **Window management** | Create additional `WebviewWindow` instances for pop‑outs, devtools, or splash screens; set `visible: false` until ready. | Avoids flash‑of‑unstyled‑content and enables multi‑monitor workflows. | | **Updater** | Use Tauri’s built‑in **updater** (v1) or **tauri-updater** (v2) with a signed JSON manifest hosted on HTTPS. | Secure, delta‑capable auto‑updates without external services. | | **Testing** | • Unit‑test Rust logic with `cargo test`.
• Integration‑test the JS↔Rust bridge using **tauri-driver** + **WebDriverIO**. | Catches FFI mismatches early. | | **Bundling** | `tauri build` produces `.msi`/`.exe` (Windows), `.dmg`/`.app` (macOS), `.AppImage`/`.deb` (Linux). Sign artifacts with `codesign` (macOS) and `signtool` (Windows). | Meets OS gatekeeper / SmartScreen requirements. | ### Notable releases | Version | Release date | Highlights | |---------|--------------|------------| | **Tauri 2.0.0‑rc.0** | **12 May 2024** | New **Capability** system replaces `allowlist`; Vite‑first frontend template; `tauri-plugin-store` v2; experimental **mobile** (iOS/Android) scaffolding; Rust 2021 edition baseline. → | | **Tauri 1.5.0** | 18 Oct 2023 | Added **sidecar** support, `tauri-plugin-sql` (SQLite), `tauri-plugin-fs` scoped API, improved macOS notarization flow. → | | **Tauri 1.4.0** | 28 Jun 2023 | WebView2 fixed‑version bootstrapper on Windows, `tauri-plugin-updater` v1.1 with delta updates, `tauri-plugin-clipboard-manager`. → | | **Tauri 1.3.0** | 14 Mar 2023 | First stable **mobile** preview (Android), `tauri-plugin-http` with rustls backend, improved `tauri::generate_context!` macro. → | ### Performance techniques (Tauri) 1. **Minimize IPC payload** – Serialize only what the UI needs; use `serde::Serialize` with `#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")]`. Large JSON round‑trips dominate latency. 2. **Batch commands** – Instead of N `invoke('getItem')` calls, expose a single `invoke('getItems', { ids })` returning a `Vec`. Reduces WebView↔Rust context switches. 3. **Lazy‑load heavy Rust crates** – Feature‑gate optional crates (e.g., `image`, `sqlx`) behind Cargo features; compile only what the current platform needs. 4. **Use `tauri::async_runtime::spawn`** for CPU‑bound work (image processing, crypto) so the Tokio executor can run it on a blocking thread pool (`spawn_blocking`). 5. **Enable `webview2` fixed version** on Windows (`"windows": { "webviewInstallMode": { "type": "fixedVersion", "version": "124.0.2478.51" } }`) to avoid runtime download stalls. 6. **Profile with `tracing` + `tracing-chrome`** – Instrument Rust commands with `#[tracing::instrument]`; open the generated `trace.json` in Chrome DevTools to see async spans. → 7. **Frontend bundle size** – Apply the same React/TS/Vite optimizations (code‑splitting, tree‑shaking, `esbuild` minify). Tauri’s binary size is ~3 MB (stripped) + WebView; the JS bundle dominates download size. 8. **Memory hygiene** – Drop large `Vec`/`String` buffers after sending to JS; use `Arc<[u8]>` for shared read‑only data to avoid clones. --- ## 4️⃣ Desktop Web‑App Development (Cross‑cutting) ### Architecture patterns | Pattern | When to use | Tooling | |---------|-------------|---------| | **Single‑page app + Tauri/Electron** | Rich interactive UI, need native APIs (FS, tray, auto‑start). | Vite + React/TS + Tauri (or Electron Forge). | | **Multi‑window / multi‑process** | Separate concerns (main UI, settings, background worker). | Tauri `WebviewWindow` + `tauri::async_runtime::spawn`; Electron `BrowserWindow` + `UtilityProcess`. | | **Local‑first data** | Offline‑first, sync later (CRDT, Yjs, Automerge). | `yjs` + `y-websocket`/`y-webrtc`; Tauri `tauri-plugin-sql` for SQLite persistence. | | **Plugin architecture** | Extensible app (e.g., IDE, design tool). | Rust `dyn Plugin` trait + `libloading` for dynamic libs; or JS plugin system via `import()` + CSP‑compatible eval. | | **Secure IPC** | Zero‑trust between web content and native layer. | Tauri’s **Capability** system; Electron’s `contextBridge` + `sandbox: true`. | ### Notable 2023‑2024 releases affecting desktop web apps | Project | Version / Date | What changed | |---------|----------------|--------------| | **Vite 5.2** | 14 Mar 2024 | Native **Lightning CSS** minifier, improved `build.cssCodeSplit`, experimental **Rolldown** Rust bundler integration. → | | **Vite 6.0 (beta)** | 30 May 2024 | **Rolldown** as default bundler (Rust‑based, ~10× faster), built‑in **SWC** transpilation, `server.middlewareMode` for SSR frameworks. → | | **Electron 28.0.0** | 23 Jan 2024 | Chromium 120, V8 12.0, `utilityProcess` stable, `webContents.setBackgroundThrottling(false)`. → | | **Electron 29.0.0** | 23 Apr 2024 | Chromium 122, `nativeImage.createThumbnailFromPath`, improved `session.clearCache()`. → | | **Wails v2.7** | 11 Feb 2024 | Go‑based alternative; new `runtime.WindowSetSystemProxy`, improved macOS notarization. → | | **Neutralinojs 4.12** | 5 Mar 2024 | Lightweight (no Chromium), new `customProtocol` for virtual FS, static binary < 3 MB. → | ### Performance‑focused techniques (desktop web apps) 1. **Startup latency** * **Preload script** – Load only the minimal JS needed to show a splash screen; defer the rest with `import()` after `window.onload`. * **Vite `build.modulePreload`** – Generates `` for entry chunks. * **Tauri `bundle > macOS > minimumSystemVersion` / Windows `webviewInstallMode.fixedVersion`** – Guarantees the WebView runtime is present, avoiding first‑run download. 2. **Runtime memory** * Enable **`process.model: "shared"`** in Electron (or Tauri’s single‑process model) only when you need true isolation; otherwise keep a single renderer to share V8 heap. * Use **`webContents.setBackgroundThrottling(false)`** sparingly; throttle background tabs to reduce CPU. * Periodically call `global.gc()` (Electron `--js-flags="--expose-gc"`) in long‑running background windows. 3. **Rendering throughput** * **`requestAnimationFrame`** for animations; avoid `setInterval`/`setTimeout` for visual updates. * **CSS `will-change`** on layers that animate; promote to GPU via `transform: translateZ(0)`. * **Virtualized lists** (`react-window`, `@tanstack/virtual`) for any list > 100 items. 4. **IPC / bridge overhead** * **Batch calls** (see Tauri section) – same principle applies to Electron `ipcRenderer.invoke`. * **Structured clone** – Prefer `postMessage`/`ipcRenderer.postMessage` with `Transferable` (ArrayBuffer) for large binary data. 5. **Disk I/O** * Use **SQLite (via `tauri-plugin-sql` or `better-sqlite3` in Electron)** with WAL mode (`PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL;`) for concurrent reads/writes. * Stream large files with `fs.createReadStream` → `ReadableStream` → `fetch`/`Response` to avoid loading whole file into memory. 6. **Profiling toolbox** * **Chrome DevTools** (attach to Tauri/Electron renderer via `--remote-debugging-port=9222`). * **`perf` / ` Instruments`** for native Rust/Go/C++ side. * **`tracy`** (Rust) + **`tracy-ui`** for nanosecond‑resolution CPU/GPU timeline. → * **`vite-plugin-inspect`** to visualise bundle graph and chunk sizes. → 7. **Distribution size** * **`tauri build --target aarch64-apple-darwin`** + `strip` → ~3 MB binary. * **Electron Forge `maker-squirrel` + `electron-updater`** with **differential updates** (binary delta ~10‑20 % of full size). * **Compress with `upx --best`** on Linux/Windows binaries (often 30‑40 % reduction). --- ### Quick “cheat‑sheet” command list (June 2024) ```bash # React + TS + Vite + Tauri (v2 RC) starter npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react-ts cd my-app npm i -D @tauri-apps/cli@next # pulls v2 RC npm i @tauri-apps/api npx tauri init # choose "Vite" + "React" # Edit tauri.conf.json → capabilities, allowlist, bundle identifiers npm run tauri dev # hot‑reload both Rust & TS npm run tauri build # produces signed installers ``` ```bash # Electron 29 + Vite + React (if you prefer Electron) npm create vite@latest my-elec -- --template react-ts cd my-elec npm i -D electron@29 electron-builder vite-plugin-electron # Add electron-builder config in package.json → "build": { "appId": "com.my.app", ... } npm run dev # Vite + Electron (via vite-plugin-electron) npm run build # produces .dmg/.exe/.AppImage ``` ```bash # Profiling a Tauri command cargo install flamegraph cargo flamegraph --bin my-tauri-app -- command_that_is_slow # Open flamegraph.svg in browser ``` --- **All links above are live as of 24 June 2024.** Use them to dive deeper into any specific area.
